paragraphs: Distributed training spreads optimization across workers, making communication part of the cost of learning. Second-order methods use curvature information and can potentially converge with fewer communication rounds. Their difficulty is that computing and communicating a large Hessian matrix can be expensive enough to undermine that advantage.

This paper proposes a distributed algorithm for generalized linear models that requires each worker to compute only diagonal blocks of the Hessian. These blocks provide an approximation to the full curvature information. The algorithm handles the resulting modeling errors through an adaptive auxiliary model, adjusting it dynamically in a way related to trust-region methods.

The authors establish convergence rates for a broad class of problems, including objectives with L1 regularization, and report state-of-the-art results on several large benchmark datasets. The contribution connects a more manageable curvature representation with an explicit mechanism for compensating for its inaccuracies. Its practical promise is to make second-order distributed training useful without requiring workers to construct the full Hessian.
icml-2018-a-distributed-second-order-alg.tldr: A distributed training algorithm uses local Hessian blocks and adaptive modeling to make second-order optimization more practical.

paragraphs: Block-coordinate optimization divides the variables into groups and updates selected groups during training. A central question is whether one particularly difficult block must control the convergence time of the entire method. Previously, alternating minimization with two blocks was known to avoid dependence on the least smooth block.

The paper shows that this favorable property can extend beyond two blocks. Its algorithm, Alternating Randomized Block Coordinate Descent, has convergence time that does not scale with the smoothness of the least smooth block. That block can even be nonsmooth, provided it can be optimized exactly. Exact optimization is also an assumption behind the corresponding two-block result.

The basic method brings alternating minimization and randomized block coordinate gradient descent into one framework, and the authors also introduce an accelerated version. The result identifies exact optimization of the difficult block as a sufficient condition for this convergence property beyond the two-block setting. It does not remove the requirement to solve that block accurately.
icml-2018-alternating-randomized-block-c.tldr: AR-BCD extends convergence independent of the least smooth block beyond two blocks, provided that block can be optimized exactly.

paragraphs: Policy iteration alternates between improving a policy and evaluating how well it performs. Earlier analyses had explored several ways to extend the evaluation stage, including returns that span multiple steps. The improvement stage raises a separate question: what happens when choosing a better policy involves looking several steps ahead?

This paper develops an analysis of that multiple-step improvement process. The authors define variants of lookahead policy improvement, turn those definitions into algorithms, and prove convergence. This gives the improvement stage its own theoretical treatment, rather than treating all uses of multiple steps as changes to policy evaluation.

The framework also encompasses recent prominent reinforcement learning algorithms as particular instances. That connection helps explain their reported empirical success through a shared mathematical structure. The contribution therefore serves two purposes: it analyzes existing approaches and supplies a way to derive additional algorithms. The abstract presents those future algorithms as candidates for study, rather than claiming that every possible extension will perform better.
icml-2018-beyond-the-one-step-greedy-app.tldr: The paper formalizes multiple-step policy improvement, proves convergence for derived algorithms, and connects existing methods through a common framework.

paragraphs: Hyperparameter search becomes expensive when each configuration requires a long training run. Bayesian optimization guides the search, but the abstract argues that its vanilla form is typically computationally infeasible for costly modern deep learning models. Bandit-based evaluation methods address resource allocation, yet approaches built on random search lack comparable guidance toward promising configurations.

BOHB combines Bayesian optimization with bandit-based methods to bring these advantages together. Its goal is useful performance even when search stops early, alongside fast progress toward optimal configurations as more resources become available. This joins the question of which configurations to explore with the question of how to evaluate them efficiently.

The authors report consistent improvements over Bayesian optimization and Hyperband across a broad collection of tested problems. These include toy functions, support vector machines, several neural network families, and deep reinforcement learning. The findings support the method's versatility across those settings. The abstract also emphasizes conceptual simplicity and ease of implementation, positioning BOHB as a practical approach to expensive configuration search.
icml-2018-bohb-robust-and-efficient-hype.tldr: BOHB combines Bayesian guidance with bandit-based evaluation and reports strong hyperparameter search performance across diverse problems.

paragraphs: The paper studies how much computation is needed to approximate the optimal transport distance between two discrete distributions, each of size n. The target accuracy is epsilon, so a smaller epsilon asks for a more precise answer. The analysis compares algorithms through bounds on their required arithmetic operations.

For a Sinkhorn-based algorithm, the authors establish a bound proportional to n²/epsilon², ignoring polylogarithmic factors. Their Adaptive Primal-Dual Accelerated Gradient Descent approach has a bound given by the smaller of n^(9/4)/epsilon and n²/epsilon², with the same convention. Both improve the accuracy dependence of the cited earlier n²/epsilon³ bound.

The minimum in the accelerated method's bound matters: the potential improvement depends jointly on distribution size and requested precision. Its contribution is therefore more specific than an unconditional claim of faster execution. The second approach also supports regularizers beyond entropic regularization. Together, the results offer improved theoretical computational guarantees and a more flexible route to regularized optimal transport.
icml-2018-computational-optimal-transpor.tldr: The paper improves optimal transport complexity bounds and introduces an accelerated approach that also supports different regularizers.

paragraphs: When several reinforcement learning agents learn concurrently in a common environment, exploration becomes a team-level problem. Adding agents raises the question of whether their combined experience makes each agent learn more efficiently. The paper examines what exploration strategies need in order to benefit from this concurrent setting.

The authors identify three necessary properties: adaptivity, commitment, and diversity. In plain terms, these concern responding to information, sustaining exploratory choices, and maintaining differences across agents' exploration. They show that straightforward extensions of single-agent optimistic methods and posterior sampling do not satisfy all three requirements.

Their proposed alternative, seed sampling, extends posterior sampling in a way that meets the identified requirements. Simulations examine how regret per agent changes as the team grows and show substantial advantages over alternative exploration schemes. These findings support coordinated exploration as an algorithmic design problem in its own right. Satisfying the three properties motivates the method, while the reported performance advantage comes from the simulations.
icml-2018-coordinated-exploration-in-con.tldr: Seed sampling coordinates concurrent agents' exploration through adaptivity, commitment, and diversity, with substantial advantages in simulations.

paragraphs: A reinforcement learning agent can observe reward changes caused by factors outside its control. Such exogenous variation can obscure the effects of its decisions and slow learning. This paper asks when those factors can be separated from the part of the problem that depends on the agent's actions.

The authors formalize exogenous state variables and rewards, then give conditions for decomposing the original decision process. One component is an exogenous Markov reward process, containing the external state and reward. The other is an endogenous decision process defined using only endogenous rewards. This provides a principled basis for separating the two sources of variation.

They also derive a variance-covariance condition under which Monte Carlo policy evaluation becomes faster on the endogenous process. Broader speedups across reinforcement learning algorithms are presented as likely, rather than established universally. Two algorithms discover exogenous variables, and experiments on several decision processes find them practical and capable of substantial acceleration. The theoretical speedup remains tied to the stated condition.
icml-2018-discovering-and-removing-exoge.tldr: The paper identifies when uncontrollable state and reward variation can be separated out to accelerate reinforcement learning.

paragraphs: Several structured prediction tasks can be expressed as choosing a weighted matching between two sets. Examples in the abstract include ranking, language-processing correspondences, and tracking multiple objects. Requiring a perfect matching creates difficulties for learning methods that otherwise offer attractive computational or statistical properties.

Conditional random fields provide statistical consistency, but normalizing their distribution over matchings requires a matrix permanent computation, which is #P-hard. Structured support vector machines offer computational efficiency but lack Fisher consistency. Consequently, for some data distributions they cannot recover the optimal matching even with the true distribution and an unrestricted choice of measurable potential functions.

The paper introduces adversarial bipartite matching to address both drawbacks. The authors develop an algorithm, establish computational efficiency and Fisher consistency, and demonstrate empirical benefits on matching problems. Fisher consistency concerns ideal learning conditions; it supports the suitability of the learning formulation rather than guaranteeing perfect predictions from finite data. The contribution combines that statistical property with an efficient computational approach.
icml-2018-efficient-and-consistent-adver.tldr: Adversarial bipartite matching combines computational efficiency with Fisher consistency for structured prediction under perfect-matching constraints.

paragraphs: This paper interprets Entropy-SGD as optimizing a PAC-Bayes risk bound for a randomized classifier formed by perturbing learned weights. The problem is that it optimizes the bound's prior using training data, violating the theorem's requirement that the prior be chosen independently. Available implementations can rapidly fit random labels, including through the associated randomized classifier.

The authors pursue valid bounds through stochastic gradient Langevin dynamics, or SGLD. They rely on a result allowing data-dependent priors when SGLD's target distribution satisfies epsilon-differential privacy. This supplies a conditional route to justifying a learned prior, rather than treating dependence on training data as automatically acceptable.

On MNIST and CIFAR10, observed test errors lie within empirically informative risk bounds calculated under the assumption that SGLD reaches stationarity. Entropy-SGLD can produce relatively tight bounds while still fitting real labels. However, the settings that yield these bounds do not achieve state-of-the-art performance. The findings connect generalization guarantees to explicit privacy and stationarity requirements, alongside an observed performance tradeoff.
icml-2018-entropy-sgd-optimizes-the-prio.tldr: The paper exposes an invalid prior choice in Entropy-SGD's PAC-Bayes interpretation and develops conditional generalization bounds using SGLD.

paragraphs: Neural network training searches for low values of a nonconvex loss function in a high-dimensional parameter space. Different minima can invite a picture of separate valleys, with higher loss between them. This paper investigates the relationship between minima by constructing routes through parameter space that connect them.

The authors allow continuous paths that need not follow straight lines. For the neural network architectures they study on CIFAR10 and CIFAR100, these paths remain essentially flat in both training and test loss. Allowing a path to bend changes the question from what happens along a direct interpolation to whether a low-loss connection can be found.

The findings suggest that the observed minima may be better understood as points within a connected low-loss manifold. That interpretation is deliberately tentative and rests on the constructed paths in the studied settings. Flat test loss along those paths also makes the observation relevant beyond the training objective. The paper offers evidence about landscape connectivity, rather than a universal characterization of every neural network minimum.
icml-2018-essentially-no-barriers-in-neu.tldr: Constructed paths between studied neural network minima remain nearly flat in training and test loss, suggesting connected low-loss regions.

paragraphs: The paper analyzes a one-hidden-layer convolutional network with non-overlapping inputs and ReLU activation. Both convolutional weights and output weights must be learned. Under Gaussian inputs, the authors prove that the learning problem contains a spurious local minimum, so the optimization landscape includes a misleading destination.

Despite that obstacle, gradient descent with weight normalization can recover the true parameters from random initialization with constant probability. Multiple restarts can amplify the chance of success. The same procedure also has a constant probability of reaching the spurious minimum, establishing that this minimum actually affects optimization rather than merely existing somewhere in parameter space.

A quantitative analysis separates learning into two phases: initially slow progress followed by much faster convergence after several iterations. Together, the results explain how useful recovery guarantees can coexist with a problematic local minimum. The guarantee is probabilistic and specific to the studied architecture, Gaussian input assumption, and normalized gradient procedure. A single randomly initialized run is therefore not assured to recover the true parameters.
icml-2018-gradient-descent-learns-one-hi.tldr: For a specified ReLU convolutional network with Gaussian inputs, normalized gradient descent can recover true parameters despite a reachable spurious minimum.

paragraphs: IMPALA addresses learning many tasks with one reinforcement learning agent and one shared set of parameters. This ambition increases both the amount of experience to process and the training time required. The paper focuses on an architecture that can handle that workload while using computational resources and collected data efficiently.

The architecture separates acting from learning and combines that separation with an off-policy correction called V-trace. The correction is part of how IMPALA maintains stable learning at high throughput. The authors report improved resource use on a single machine and scaling to thousands of machines without sacrificing data efficiency or resource utilization.

The evaluation covers DMLab-30 and Atari57, testing the architecture in multi-task reinforcement learning. Reported results show better performance than previous agents with less data, together with positive transfer between tasks. Positive transfer means that shared multi-task learning helps performance across tasks. These findings connect the systems design to the learning objective: scaling experience processing supports a single agent whose tasks can benefit from being learned together.
icml-2018-impala-scalable-distributed-de.tldr: IMPALA combines separate acting and learning with V-trace correction to scale multi-task reinforcement learning and achieve positive transfer.

paragraphs: People approach a new video game with knowledge about the world that can guide their decisions before they understand the game's rules. This paper investigates how much that prior knowledge contributes to efficient play. It focuses on visual information that allows players to bring useful expectations to a sample game.

The researchers modify the game environment to systematically mask different kinds of visual information. These ablation studies test how human performance changes when particular sources of prior knowledge become harder to use. The approach links changes in available information to changes in how quickly people solve the game.

Removing some information produces a large slowdown, with one reported example increasing solution time from two minutes to more than twenty. The results indicate that general expectations concerning objects and visual consistency are critical for efficient play in the investigated setting. The contribution is evidence that human game-solving speed depends substantially on prior knowledge supported by the presentation of the environment, rather than solely on learning through play.
icml-2018-investigating-human-priors-for.tldr: Masking visual cues in a sample game shows that human priors about objects and visual consistency can strongly affect solving speed.

paragraphs: Cooperative reinforcement learning becomes difficult when agents act in a decentralized setting and each has only partial information. The paper addresses this problem through decentralized partially observable Markov decision processes. Earlier approaches based on forms of generalized policy iteration could, at best, arrive at local optima.

The authors restrict learning to plans, which they describe as easier to store and update than policies. Under certain conditions, this enables a near-optimal cooperative multi-agent learning algorithm. The change in representation is central: it gives the learning procedure a simpler object to maintain while supporting a stronger conditional result.

To improve scalability, the method replaces greedy maximization with mixed-integer linear programming. Experiments show that it can learn near-optimal behavior in many finite domains from the literature. The theoretical claim depends on conditions, and the empirical claim concerns the tested finite domains. Together, they show that plan-based learning and a different optimization procedure can make near-optimal decentralized cooperation achievable in the settings studied.
icml-2018-learning-to-act-in-decentraliz.tldr: A plan-based approach gives conditional near-optimal cooperative learning guarantees and uses mixed-integer programming to improve scalability.

paragraphs: Approximate linear algebra supports large-scale tasks such as regression, matrix multiplication, and low-rank approximation. Much of the distributed and streaming work in this area had focused on the Euclidean norm, or l2. This paper extends attention to other lp norms, allowing different ways of measuring approximation error.

The choice of norm matters because norms with p below two offer greater robustness, while those with p above two can help identify outliers. The authors give deterministic algorithms that work simultaneously for every p at least one, including infinity. They also show that the algorithms can operate in both streaming and distributed environments.

The problems studied include lp regression, entrywise lp low-rank approximation, and versions of approximate matrix multiplication. The contribution brings together breadth of norm coverage, determinism, and compatibility with two important large-data settings. This makes the framework relevant when Euclidean error is not the desired criterion, while retaining the ability to process data through streaming or distributed computation.
icml-2018-leveraging-well-conditioned-ba.tldr: The paper develops deterministic streaming and distributed algorithms for approximate linear algebra across all lp norms with p at least one.

paragraphs: The paper studies optimization over matrices that must simultaneously be symmetric, positive semidefinite, and stochastic. These combined requirements create a structured feasible set. The authors develop a Riemannian optimization framework that uses the geometry of that set to formulate and solve the problem.

They replace the matrix variable X with a factorization YYᵀ and derive conditions on the number of columns of Y under which this representation produces a satisfactory solution. The resulting problem can be expressed on either an embedded or a quotient Riemannian manifold. The paper works out tangent spaces, Riemannian gradients, and a retraction operator, providing the ingredients needed to construct optimization algorithms.

Numerical results in graph clustering show a clear complexity advantage over compared Euclidean and Riemannian methods when the optimal solution has a known low rank. That qualification is central to the reported benefit: the factorization exploits the solution's low-rank structure. The contribution combines conditions on the representation with explicit geometric tools and evidence of computational advantages in that setting.
icml-2018-low-rank-riemannian-optimizati.tldr: A matrix-factorization and Riemannian framework offers computational advantages for graph clustering when the optimal solution has a known low rank.

paragraphs: Compressed sensing reconstructs a signal from a small number of linear measurements by exploiting assumptions about its structure. A domain-specific generative model can supply a strong prior and reduce the measurements needed. However, existing generative approaches guarantee exact recovery only for signals within the model's support, which may cover little of the overall signal space.

Sparse-Gen allows a signal to deviate sparsely from that support. It therefore combines a domain-specific generative prior with a way to represent departures from what the generator can produce. This expands the reconstruction framework beyond the generator's support without discarding the structure supplied by the model.

The theoretical framework introduces a class of signals suitable for compressed sensing and includes classical sparse-vector recovery as a special case. Experiments report consistent reconstruction improvements over competing approaches, especially in transfer compressed sensing. In that setting, a generator learned from a data-rich source domain helps sensing in a data-scarce target domain, where allowing deviations from the source model is particularly useful.
icml-2018-modeling-sparse-deviations-for.tldr: Sparse-Gen combines generative priors with sparse deviations to broaden compressed-sensing reconstruction beyond a generator's support.

paragraphs: Off-policy evaluation estimates how well a policy would perform using data collected by other policies. Doubly robust estimators combine importance sampling with a performance model, seeking the low bias of the former and low variance of the latter. The quality of that model can strongly influence the final estimate.

This paper focuses on how to train the model component. Its more robust doubly robust estimators choose model parameters by minimizing the variance of the complete estimator. That objective directly connects model learning to the reliability of policy evaluation, addressing an aspect that earlier work had emphasized less than improving importance sampling.

The authors derive variance formulas for contextual bandits and reinforcement learning whose gradients with respect to model parameters can be estimated from samples. They then propose efficient variance-minimization methods and prove strong consistency and asymptotic optimality. Evaluations compare the approach with existing methods on bandit and reinforcement learning benchmarks. The central contribution is an estimator-focused learning objective backed by theoretical guarantees about its large-sample behavior.
icml-2018-more-robust-doubly-robust-off-.tldr: MRDR trains the model inside a doubly robust estimator to minimize evaluation variance, with consistency and asymptotic optimality guarantees.

paragraphs: Recurrent neural networks are useful for sequential data such as text and speech, but they can overfit their training examples. Noisin addresses this through regularization that injects random noise into the network's hidden states. Training then maximizes the corresponding marginal likelihood of the observed data.

The method is unbiased in the specific sense that the underlying recurrent network is preserved on average. Individual noisy computations can differ, while their average retains the original network. The authors show how the method applies to any RNN, examine multiple noise types, and characterize its regularizing effect through both theory and experiments.

On language-modeling benchmarks, the paper reports improvements over dropout of up to 12.2% on Penn Treebank and 9.4% on Wikitext-2. It also compares a state-of-the-art language model with and without Noisin, finding that the version using Noisin reaches state-of-the-art performance sooner on Penn Treebank. These results support hidden-state noise as a useful regularization approach in the tested language-modeling settings.
icml-2018-noisin-unbiased-regularization.tldr: Noisin regularizes recurrent networks with hidden-state noise that preserves the underlying network on average and improves tested language models.

paragraphs: This paper studies why adding parameters can make neural networks easier to learn. Its theoretical setting is a shallow network with quadratic activation, k hidden nodes, and n training examples. For general smooth convex losses, the authors show that k at least the square root of 2n is sufficient for local search to find a globally optimal solution.

The analysis links this amount of over-parametrization to favorable properties of the loss landscape. Its proof uses an idea from smoothed analysis, which the authors suggest may also help study other neural network loss surfaces. The width condition supplies a sufficient guarantee in the specified setting; it is not presented as a necessary threshold for successful learning.

The paper separately addresses generalization when the parameter count can exceed the sample count. Using Rademacher complexity, it establishes good generalization with weight decay when data come from a regular distribution such as a Gaussian. Thus, the optimization and generalization conclusions rely on distinct stated conditions, connecting additional capacity to both trainability and controlled predictive behavior.
icml-2018-on-the-power-of-over-parametri.tldr: For shallow quadratic networks, sufficient width enables global optimization by local search, with conditional generalization guarantees under weight decay.

paragraphs: K-core decomposition is a graph-analysis primitive used in machine learning and data mining. Applying it at scale raises questions about memory use and how many times computation must revisit or exchange information about the graph. This paper develops approximate decomposition methods for streaming and distributed environments.

The central tool is a new sketching technique for k-core decomposition. The authors show how to compute the sketch efficiently in streaming and MapReduce models, using it to compute and maintain an approximate decomposition with provable guarantees. Their analysis bounds space consumption as well as the number of passes or rounds of computation.

Those guarantees address several resource costs together, which matters when a large graph cannot be processed conveniently in one place. The paper presents these as the first distributed and streaming algorithms with the stated approximate-decomposition guarantees. Experiments on publicly available graphs support the effectiveness of the sketching technique. The outcome is a theoretically supported approximation approach with empirical evidence in practical graph settings.
icml-2018-parallel-and-streaming-algorit.tldr: A new sketching technique enables approximate k-core decomposition with provable memory and computation bounds in streaming and distributed settings.

paragraphs: State-space models describe patterns in time series through an evolving internal state and are useful for system identification. Deterministic versions have been successful on complex sequences, but fully probabilistic models can be difficult to train even on smaller problems. This paper targets that training difficulty with a new formulation and scalable algorithm.

The proposed probabilistic recurrent state-space model combines Gaussian processes with doubly stochastic variational inference. A key feature is efficient treatment of temporal correlations among latent states. The authors find that retaining these relationships across time is important for robust training, making them central to the design rather than incidental structure.

The method is evaluated on real-world benchmark datasets against state-of-the-art probabilistic model-learning approaches. A high-dimensional problem also demonstrates scalability and robustness. These findings support the combination of a probabilistic state representation and an inference procedure that accounts for temporal dependence. The abstract's central explanation for the training improvement is the effective incorporation of correlations between hidden states over time.
icml-2018-probabilistic-recurrent-state-.tldr: PR-SSM combines Gaussian processes and variational inference to train probabilistic state-space models while retaining temporal correlations.

paragraphs: The paper considers high-dimensional convex objectives made from three components with different regularity: a differentiable term, a twice-differentiable term, and a nonsmooth term. Treating each component according to its available structure motivates the randomized block cubic Newton method, or RBCN.

Each iteration builds a combined approximation. The differentiable component receives a linear model with quadratic regularization; the twice-differentiable component receives a quadratic model with cubic regularization; and the nonsmooth component is handled through its proximal model. RBCN then minimizes this combined model over a randomly selected subset of variable blocks.

The analysis gives convergence rates of O(1/epsilon), O(1/sqrt(epsilon)), and O(log(1/epsilon)) under different assumptions on the component functions. These are separate conditional results, rather than interchangeable guarantees for every objective. The method generalizes several existing approaches and matches the best known bounds in its special cases. Numerical experiments report advantages over state-of-the-art methods on problems including cubically regularized least squares, constrained logistic regression, and Poisson regression.
icml-2018-randomized-block-cubic-newton-.tldr: RBCN combines component-specific objective models with randomized block updates and provides convergence guarantees under several sets of assumptions.

paragraphs: This paper makes Gaussian process inference more scalable through a structured kernel approximation. Its GRIEF kernel uses p eigenfunctions obtained by a Nystrom approximation on a dense Cartesian grid of inducing points. The resulting representation enables computation of the log marginal likelihood and all hyperparameter derivatives in O(p) time.

The computational mechanism uses algebraic properties of Kronecker and Khatri-Rao tensor products. Exploiting that structure can make training complexity practically independent of the number of inducing points. This allows a very large inducing grid to support a globally accurate kernel approximation, including in high-dimensional problems, without making the grid size directly determine the practical training cost.

Fast likelihood evaluation enables type-I or type-II Bayesian inference on large datasets. The authors benchmark the methods on real-world problems with up to two million training points and 10^33 inducing points. The distinction between p eigenfunctions and the much larger inducing grid is central: the stated evaluation cost depends on the representation size p, while structured algebra handles the grid.
icml-2018-scalable-gaussian-processes-wi.tldr: GP-GRIEF uses grid structure and eigenfunction approximations to support fast Gaussian process likelihood calculations with enormous inducing grids.

paragraphs: Preference learning can involve finding the best item, ordering all items, or estimating every pairwise preference probability. This paper studies these three tasks in an adaptive PAC setting, where the comparison process can respond to information already collected. It asks how structural assumptions about preferences affect the required number of comparisons.

Under Weak Stochastic Transitivity, finding the best among n items requires at least order n² comparisons. With the somewhat stronger assumption of Medium Stochastic Transitivity, the authors provide a linear-complexity algorithm for the same task. This contrast shows that a change in preference structure can substantially alter the difficulty of maximum selection.

For ranking, Strong Stochastic Transitivity together with the Stochastic Triangle Inequality supports an optimal O(n log n) algorithm. Under those assumptions, the paper also gives an optimal algorithm for estimating all pairwise preference probabilities. The results connect achievable efficiency to specific assumptions, so the faster guarantees should be read together with the stronger structure that enables them.
icml-2018-the-limits-of-maxing-ranking-a.tldr: The paper shows how preference assumptions determine comparison complexity for selecting the best item, ranking, and estimating pairwise probabilities.
